blocks.text: Mean Encoding closed the leakage and overfitting gaps in target based encoding, but it, like every technique covered earlier in this module, genuinely still requires knowing the full set of categories in advance, and its column count, or lookup table size, genuinely still grows alongside the number of distinct categories. Hash encoding, the final topic in this module, breaks that pattern entirely, using a fixed number of output columns regardless of how many categories actually exist.

This topic covers exactly how a hash function maps categories into a fixed set of buckets, the genuinely extreme cardinality cases where this becomes necessary, a real, practical advantage this technique has over every other one covered in this module, handling brand new categories automatically, the real cost of hash collisions, the genuine loss of interpretability this technique carries, and the tradeoff involved in choosing how many buckets to use.
1. How Hash Encoding Actually Works

blocks.alt: A category passes through a hash function into a fixed bucket

blocks.text: A raw category value is passed through a genuine hash function, a deterministic function that converts any input into a number, and that number is then mapped into one of a genuinely fixed number of output buckets, columns, decided in advance, regardless of how many distinct categories actually exist in the data. Two rows with the same category value genuinely always hash into the same bucket, keeping the encoding consistent.

This is a genuinely fundamental shift from every technique covered earlier in this module, there is no lookup table to build or maintain, and no need to ever know the complete list of possible categories ahead of time at all.
2. Genuinely Extreme Cardinality Cases

blocks.alt: Millions of categories map through hash encoding into a fixed number of buckets

blocks.text: User IDs in a genuinely large system can easily number in the millions, and URLs form a genuinely unbounded, constantly growing set of possible values, new ones appearing every day. Even binary encoding, with its genuinely favorable log base 2 column scaling covered earlier in this module, still struggles at this scale, millions of categories would still require roughly 20 binary columns, and still require knowing the complete category list up front.

Hash encoding genuinely handles both of these extreme cases directly, the output size stays exactly the same, a handful of buckets, whether the underlying category count is a hundred or a hundred million.
3. A Worked Example
Applying scikit-learn FeatureHasher to a small set of category values shows the fixed size output directly, regardless of how many distinct categories are actually present.

code.content:
from sklearn.feature_extraction import FeatureHasher

categories = [{"user_id": "u10293"}, {"user_id": "u88213"}, {"user_id": "u10293"}]

hasher = FeatureHasher(n_features=8, input_type="dict")
hashed = hasher.transform(categories)

print(hashed.toarray())

blocks.text: Every output here genuinely has exactly 8 columns, n_features, regardless of how many genuinely distinct user IDs actually exist, whether that count were 3, as here, or 3 million in a real production system.

blocks.title: A related, real connection
blocks.content: HashingVectorizer, briefly mentioned back in Text Features, applies this genuine same hashing trick specifically to text tokens, exactly the same underlying idea covered here, applied to a different, unstructured data type.

blocks.text: 4. A Real, Practical Advantage: Handling Unseen Categories

blocks.alt: A brand new category still falls into an existing bucket through the hash function

blocks.text: Every technique covered earlier in this module, label encoding, ordinal encoding, one-hot encoding, all genuinely need explicit handling for a brand new category appearing later in production, exactly the unseen category risk first flagged back in Label Encoding. Hash encoding genuinely sidesteps this problem entirely, the hash function computes a bucket for any input at all, seen before or not, with no lookup table to fail to find a match in.

This is a genuinely real, practical advantage specific to this technique, in a genuinely streaming or online context, new user IDs or URLs appearing constantly, hash encoding continues working correctly without any retraining or explicit unseen category handling required at all.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Hash encoding is the only technique in this entire module that genuinely handles a brand new, unseen category automatically, with no special configuration or fallback logic required at all.

blocks.text: 5. The Real Cost: Hash Collisions

blocks.alt: Two different categories can collide into the same bucket

blocks.text: Because a genuinely fixed, limited number of buckets must represent a potentially unlimited number of categories, two genuinely distinct categories can occasionally hash into the exact same bucket, a real collision. Once that happens, those two genuinely different categories become indistinguishable to a model from that point forward, a genuine, real loss of information with no direct way to detect or reverse it after the fact.

This is a genuinely different, and arguably more opaque, collision risk than the one covered back in Frequency Encoding, there, two categories sharing a frequency was at least directly, visibly inspectable, a hash collision happens silently, hidden inside the hash function internal computation.

blocks.text: 6. No Genuine Interpretability at All

blocks.alt: A hashed column cannot be interpreted directly

blocks.text: A one-hot encoded column, is_red, genuinely means exactly one clear thing. Even a binary encoded column, while harder to interpret alone, at least corresponds to a genuine, specific bit of a real category code. A hash encoded column, bucket 47, genuinely means nothing at all on its own, it is not even reliably tied to a consistent, describable pattern the way a binary encoded bit is.

This is genuinely the steepest interpretability cost of any technique covered in this entire module, worth accepting only when the real, practical benefits, fixed size and automatic handling of unseen categories, genuinely outweigh the loss of any meaningful, human readable interpretation of the resulting columns.

blocks.text: 7. Choosing the Number of Buckets

blocks.alt: Few buckets mean more collisions while many buckets mean fewer collisions

blocks.text: More buckets genuinely reduce the chance of a collision, since categories are spread across more possible destinations, but a genuinely larger bucket count also moves the technique back toward the same column count problem that motivated moving away from one-hot encoding in the first place. Fewer buckets stay genuinely more compact, but at the real cost of more frequent collisions.

This is a genuine, real hyperparameter decision, one best made empirically by testing a few candidate bucket counts and checking downstream model performance, exactly the kind of systematic search covered in far more depth in the Hyperparameter Tuning module later in this course.
8. Closing Out the Encoding Techniques Module

blocks.alt: The Encoding Techniques module is complete, Handling Imbalanced Data comes next

blocks.text: Hash encoding completes this module, which began with the genuine dangers of label encoding false ordering, moved through the safe, structural alternatives of one-hot and binary encoding, then into the feature only strategies of frequency and count encoding, and finally into the more powerful but carefully managed target and mean encoding, ending here with this genuinely final answer to extreme cardinality.

Every categorical column a real dataset might contain, from a handful of clean values to millions of ever changing ones, now has a genuine, appropriate technique available from this module toolkit. The next module, Handling Imbalanced Data, addresses a genuinely different, equally common real world challenge, what to do when a target class itself is rare, regardless of how its features happen to be encoded.

items: Hash encoding passes a category through a hash function into a genuinely fixed number of output buckets.
It genuinely handles extreme cardinality, like millions of user IDs or URLs, that other techniques struggle with.
It is the only technique in this module that genuinely handles a brand new, unseen category automatically.
Hash collisions cause genuine, real information loss that cannot be directly inspected or reversed.
Hash encoded columns carry genuinely no interpretability at all, the steepest cost of any technique in this module.
The number of buckets is a genuine tradeoff between collision risk and output size, best tuned empirically.
